paragon

PAIR-uh-gon -- three syllables, stress on the first syllable, PAIR. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Paragon is a perfect example of something.

Critics called the restored opera house a paragon of careful preservation.

Example

At the obedience trials, one border collie proves a paragon: she sits the instant she is asked, holds her stay while squirrels sprint past, and trots to heel through a crowd of strangers. The judges simply stop taking notes.

She is the perfect example, the standard against which everything else gets measured. A paragon is not merely good -- it is the model other examples are compared to.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

exemplar: An exemplar is a clear, representative example -- the case you would pick to show what a whole group is typically like. A paragon goes further than representing well: it is the flawless best of the group, the one everything else is measured against.

standard: A standard is the level of quality something must reach -- a bar to clear, not a person or thing. A paragon does not merely meet the bar: it is the living example that embodies the quality perfectly, the one the bar could be set by.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

disgrace: a shameful example that brings dishonor

failure: something that falls far short of the standard

Where it sits · how near to perfection it stands — model → paragon → ideal

model vs. paragon: A model is worth copying -- a model student does things well -- while a paragon sits a step higher: not just worth copying but essentially flawless in that quality.

ideal vs. paragon: Ideal is the strongest concept: the ideal may exist only in imagination, while a paragon is the ideal walking around in the real world -- perfection you can actually point to.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — para-

Prefix — para-: beside, alongside (Greek)

Root — gon

Root — gon: whetstone (from Greek akone; its a merged away as the word passed into Italian paragone, 'touchstone')

Put it together

Put it together: Para- ('beside, alongside') + gon ('whetstone' — from Greek akone, whose a merged away as the word passed into Italian paragone, 'touchstone'): Greek parakonan meant 'to sharpen against,' and paragone was the touchstone used to test gold. A paragon is the touchstone in person: the example everything else is rubbed against to see if it measures up.

Where This Word Comes From

Where This Word Comes From: Paragon goes back to Greek akone, a whetstone -- the stone a blade is sharpened against. Akone built no other English word, though its ancient root ak-, 'sharp,' also lies behind everyday words like acid. Picture a paragon as the touchstone: the example everything else gets rubbed against to see whether it measures up.

Root Check

Word Choice

Paragon takes of plus the quality: a paragon of patience, of honesty, of hospitality. It is high, slightly formal praise -- and because it claims perfection, writers sometimes deploy it with a wink ('my brother, that paragon of neatness, lost his own shoes').
